Competitor Analysis Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you. AHREFS Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more. Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.     #23002. Breaking: Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1891 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Darkreading ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Darkreading

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the oldest running bug disclosure programs announced it would shorten public disclosure timelines to vendors from 120 days to 30 over the next 14 months.
    • Google will soon drastically reduce the disclosure deadlines of vulnerabilities prior to publicly disclosing them, and the move has sparked concern among some cybersecurity professionals.
    • According to recent reports, project Zero, Google's third-party vulnerability remediation program, right now follows what it describes as "90+30" policy: 90 days to remediate a vulnerability and an extra 30-day "soak time" to allow for patch rollout before publicly disclosing the bug.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the oldest running bug disclosure programs announced it would shorten public disclosure timelines to vendors from 120 days to 30 over the next 14 months.

    Google will soon drastically reduce the disclosure deadlines of vulnerabilities prior to publicly disclosing them, and the move has sparked concern among some cybersecurity professionals.

    According to recent reports, project Zero, Google's third-party vulnerability remediation program, right now follows what it describes as "90+30" policy: 90 days to remediate a vulnerability and an extra 30-day "soak time" to allow for patch rollout before publicly disclosing the bug. This will no longer be the case. As of the announcement on Nov. 13, Google changed its policy to disclose 90 days after reporting to the vendor. As of Feb. 2, 2027, vulnerabilities will be disclosed after 60 days. As of Jan. 3, 2028, vulnerabilities will be disclosed after 30 days.

    In a blog post outlining the decision, Google's Natalie Silvanovich wrote that while the intention of 90+30 was to encourage faster patching while giving vendors time to deliver patches, "The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient.".

    Related:'Sleeper Agent' Tactic Hides Payloads in Open-Weight AI Models.

    Specifically, Silvanovich noted that large language models have enabled threat actors to find and exploit vulnerabilities much faster in today's AI era.

    Industry observers note that "A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to customers than one reported last year. In this upcoming environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster," she wrote. "LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior.".

    Project Zero is not a conventional bug disclosure program. Founded in 2014, the organization was established specifically so Google could help facilitate the safe reporting and disclosure of high-severity, high-impact vulnerabilities found in widely used software and hardware. That remarked, Project Zero's move reflects a broad inundation of AI-discovered vulnerabilities, and where Google goes, the rest of the industry may follow.

    As for whether such a thing is good, bad, or necessary for the cybersecurity industry, experts appear to be split.

    Disclosure timelines are a key part of the vulnerability ecosystem. When a researcher or firm discovers a vulnerability and submits it to the software developer responsible, a standard timeline is usually designated for the developer to fix the vulnerability; such deadlines are usually 90 or 120 days, but it varies depending on the bug, disclosure policy, and circumstances.

    Related:November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs.

    Recent findings suggest that if the software developer ignores the bug report, is slow to address it, or declines to communicate with the researcher, the researcher may choose to disclose the flaw at the end of the disclosure timeline to inform security teams and practitioners of the looming threat. These timelines hold software vendors accountable and encourage them to maintain secure software, but it's not perfect science.

    Oftentimes, the researcher and software developer will work together to coordinate a disclosure date so relevant research, patches, and mitigations are ready at the same time. Sometimes, if the bug is especially dangerous or requires more time to fix, the timeline may change and the technical details and proof-of-concept exploits will be held until a later date.

    Industry observers note that it's worth noting there are no standard requirements between platforms. HackerOne keeps its default disclosure timeline to 30 days, though it's broadly set at the program level by each vendor customer, and many HackerOne programs set longer timelines. Bugcrowd researchers and vendors generally coordinate timelines; program rules again supersede standards.

    TrendAI's Zero Day Initiative (which is not a platform but a vendor-agnostic vulnerability disclosure program) uses a standard disclosure timeline of 120 days for responsive vendors that release working patches, and shorter timelines for vulnerabilities that result from faulty patches.

    It has been revealed that it remains to be seen whether the larger industry will follow Project Zero's lead. Dustin Childs, ZDI's head of threat awareness, calls Google's decision "a bold move to be sure, especially considering the explosion of bug reports coming in thanks to AI assisted discovery.".

    It has been revealed that however, he worries about how shorter timelines may impact remediation quality. "I fear it will lead to patches that don’t fully address the vulnerability. We see that happen at 120 days," Childs notes. "We’ll be watching closely to see how this change impacts vendors and researchers alike.".

    Alex Rice, cofounder, CISO, and CTO at HackerOne, tells Dark Reading that he expects the industry to move in Google's direction, though not necessarily in lockstep. He argues that patch soak time no longer protects defenders, given how quickly attackers can exploit flaws now. And because Project Zero is a disclosure program for vulnerabilities with demonstrated impact and not a bug bounty platform that addresses a broad range of flaws, Google is in a unique position to set aggressive expectations.

    Industry observers note that "The specifics will still vary by program, severity, and whether a fix is realistic, and platforms like ours will need to support that flexibility," Rice claims. "But the direction isn’t in question. Organizations should strategy for 30 days as the baseline expectation that will shrink even further.".

    Industry observers note that between stories from this year about AI models capable of discovering zero-day bugs off of human language prompts and vulnerability coordinators fighting huge spikes in bug reporting volumes the past couple of years, Google's position seems defensible. The tech giant isn't alone in its move either: In January, Anthropic's own coordinated disclosure policy will shorten from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity bugs, and 45 days for all other cases.

    But not everyone agrees. Expel principal threat researcher Marcus Hutchins took concern with the move in a post to X, where he noted that 2026 has already seen far more CVEs than 2025. "Sure, there are some vendors who just sit on bugs forever and don't make any effort to patch them. But there's way more overworked & underpaid teams, non-profits, and solo projects who are patching bugs as fast as they physically can," he wrote.

    Katie Moussouris, CEO of Luta Security and a pioneer in vulnerability disclosure, largely agrees. As she tells Dark Reading, even AI firms right now struggle to patch the issues they find, leaving volunteers and less resourced firms even further back against the wall. "A deadline doesn't magically manifest a fix.".

    Industry observers note that "Researchers and AI companies are burying maintainers in bug reports and not doing enough to help fix them. This isn't even a matter of model access or token cost. The AI companies themselves can't even close the gap," she says. "Anthropic reports that 629 of the 5,087 vulnerabilities it disclosed have been patched. OpenAI's Patch the Planet initiative, run with security engineers from Trail of Bits, has written patches for a third of the 2,055 issues it found, and 23% have been accepted upstream.".

    A Google spokesperson tells Dark Reading that in creating the new policy, the tech giant solicited feedback from the vendors Project Zero reports the most vulnerabilities to, including open source projects.

    Sources indicate that "The general consensus was that these timelines are achievable, and most open source projects are almost there," the spokesperson claims. "Every vulnerability that Project Zero reported against a volunteer-maintained project in 2026 was fixed in 30 days, except for one, which was fixed in 31 days. Open source projects are among the vendors who will need to make the fewest changes to meet our new policy, as they are already doing so well.".

    Industry observers note that while one side of the argument disagrees with the rollout of shorter timelines, the other side sees it as inevitable or necessary to respond to how attackers now use AI to pursue their goals. HackerOne's Rice claims that right now, teams are not ready to deal with a 30-day turnaround, but Google's move may offer an opportunity at the boardroom level to convince technology and executive partners that remediation is a shared responsibility.

    In a recent development, "If you're a security team struggling to keep up, don't waste time playing the victim. Take this as a gift," he states. "Ask for dedicated engineering capacity for security fixes, pre-agreed remediation SLAs, automated validation and retesting, and the authority to ship mitigations while the full fix is built. The teams that turn this pressure into that conversation will be far ahead of the ones hoping for external relief.".

    Casey Ellis, founder of Bugcrowd and The disclose.io Project, says this is a necessary evolution, even if it feels aggressive. In the wake of proliferated vulnerability discovery, the timeline shortening "puts productive pressure on response and fix pipelines.".

    Ellis states he feels the typical targets of Project Zero researchers are in "decent shape," but community norms tend to follow Google's lead on CVE timelines, so the move could carry larger impact.

    "My main concern would be companies that maintain safety-critical systems or those that are otherwise logistically difficult to enhancement; a security fix doesn't always end with a patch, and more often than not, it doesn't," he states. "The Project Zero changes will ultimately reveal (and hopefully shrink or close) the readiness gap for many PSIRT teams, products, and hosted service providers, but unless product vendors become proactive about this aspect of vulnerability discovery and disclosure it is likely to be a bumpy ride for some.".

    Senior News Writer, Dark Reading.

After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

    At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

    • As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

    Recent findings suggest that our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

    As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

    Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

    Recent findings suggest that results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where latest models are added through a PR on the Space.

    Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

    All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

    Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

    On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

    Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

    Industry observers note that -k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

    The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

    #23000. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

    📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (774 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Krebsonsecurity ↗ Open Full Page

    Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today.
    • The security firm Layer3 Intel mentioned it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650).
    • The proxy tracking firm Synthient stated on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian organization whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

    The security firm Layer3 Intel mentioned it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 revealed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

    The proxy tracking firm Synthient stated on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

    In a recent development, synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

    There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

    Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

    Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel remarked it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

    It has been revealed that “This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”.

    The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

    As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

    They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage indicated how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting owners.

    “Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”.

    All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

    Industry observers note that as risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end owners, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox mentioned it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

    #22998. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1728 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one.
    • According to recent reports, both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language.
    • It has been revealed that palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

    According to recent reports, both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

    It has been revealed that palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

    A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

    According to recent reports, it lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

    It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

    Sources indicate that there's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

    According to recent reports, nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one indicates, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:.

    Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

    We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

    There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

    Recent findings suggest that every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and indicates why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:.

    "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance.".

    The coder reasons about geometry:.

    "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart.".

    Sources indicate that the teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

    The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

    According to recent reports, what fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

    People often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the proposal and wrapped in [[ ]]:.

    The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

    The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

    In a recent development, figure 1. An illustration of the same proposal without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

    Sources indicate that even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

    Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

    First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

    Sources indicate that the key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

    It has been revealed that figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

    Recent findings suggest that to measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

    Industry observers note that we evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a initiative, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

    Industry observers note that figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

    Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

    Sources indicate that presentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

    Recent findings suggest that the harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

    We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

    Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:.

    #22996. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1284 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.
    • It has been revealed that in April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms.
    • OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

    It has been revealed that in April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

    OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

    Sources indicate that however, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

    Industry observers note that run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

    According to recent reports, A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that promptly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

    So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

    Recent findings suggest that say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:.

    The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

    Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

    The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

    The data is organized into three streams:.

    All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

    The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

    We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

    Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

    In a recent development, cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

    This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

    SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

    On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

    In a recent development, on a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

    A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

    In a recent development, this isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

    Sources indicate that parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

    It has been revealed that try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

    Is sharenting safe? 7 ways to mindfully post about your kids online

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1433 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that clinically reviewed by Dr.
    • Sources indicate that your kid loses their first tooth or notes something hilarious at dinner, and your thumb is already halfway to the share button.
    • Believe it or not, there's actually a name for this habit: sharenting.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

    Sources indicate that your kid loses their first tooth or notes something hilarious at dinner, and your thumb is already halfway to the share button. For a lot of parents and caregivers, posting these moments feels like second nature.

    Believe it or not, there's actually a name for this habit: sharenting. And while it’s often a simple way to stay connected, it also puts your child’s story online before they can choose to share it. If you’ve started to wonder about the risks, it’s a good time to take stock of your posting habits.

    Here's a look at why parents share and what’s worth knowing about the risks, plus seven small shifts to help you post with confidence.

    Sharenting is when parents or caregivers post about their kids on social media. It could be a single birthday photo, or years of posts documenting a whole childhood. Think videos, funny quotes, school updates, potty-training wins, and even ultrasound pictures from before the baby arrives.

    According to recent reports, it's also widespread. Research reviews estimate that about three in four parents share photos, stories, or videos of their kids online, and most use their children's real names.

    Parents have always shared news about their kids through holiday letters, birth announcements, and photos mailed to relatives. Social media just made the audience much bigger, the posts more public, and the record harder to remove.

    Most sharenting comes from a good place. You're proud of your kid and you want the people in your life to know. Studies on parents who post about their kids point to the same reasons:.

    Staying close: Photos and videos let faraway family and friends watch your child grow.

    Celebrating and remembering: Posts mark your child’s milestones and give you something to scroll back through later.

    Finding community: Other parents and caregivers can offer advice and a “me too” at 2am, when parenting feels isolating.

    Feeling seen: A kind comment on a rough day reminds you that you’re doing okay.

    💙 Feeling alone as a parent? Here’s how to deal with loneliness.

    Sharing your kids online isn’t necessarily harmful. Still, a few risks are worth knowing about:.

    Industry observers note that A lasting digital footprint. Screenshots, reshares, and archives mean a photo can outlast the original post. Many kids have years of photos online before they're old enough to understand who can see them.

    According to recent reports, privacy and consent. Young kids can't weigh in on what you post about them. Their public image takes shape long before they can agree to it, and that can be hard to undo later.

    Personal information. Someone could piece together a full name, birth date, hometown, and school from a handful of posts. Over time, details like these may be misused for identity theft.

    In a recent development, location and background details. Location tags and details like a house number, school logo, or regular park in the background show where your child spends their time. On a public account, that can make their routine visible to strangers.

    According to recent reports, facial recognition and AI. Photos on public accounts may be saved, scanned, or collected by AI tools and facial recognition software. Some of those tools turn ordinary photos into fake images.

    It has been revealed that 💙 Want to bring more intention to parenting, online and off? Start here.

    Sources indicate that you don't have to log off to keep your kid safe. A few small shifts protect their privacy and still let you share the moments you love. Start with one or two of these, whatever feels most doable, then add more as they become habit.

    Before you hit share, take a breath and think about whether you want to post this moment. If you do, scan the photo and caption for anything that gives away too much, like a full name or a street sign.

    For some structure, a short breathing exercise or meditation can help.

    💙 Listen to Pause to Breathe with Prof. Megan Reitz on Calm.

    A couple of settings are worth checking before your next post. If your account is public, anyone can find and save your posts. Photos taken on your phone may also include the location where you took them.

    Switch to a private account and remove followers you don’t know.

    Turn off geotagging in your camera and app settings.

    Platforms can change their defaults without warning, so it’s worth redoing this check every couple of months.

    According to recent reports, you can share the moment without giving away your child’s identity. Skip birth dates, school names, and daily routines. Use a nickname or first initial instead of your child’s full name.

    Posting a day or two later makes it harder for anyone to know where your child is in real time.

    Once your child is old enough to weigh in, show them the post and ask if they're okay with you sharing it. This shows them that their opinion matters. If your child is too young to decide, the next tip can help you decide for them.

    Imagine your child at 25, seeing what you’re about to post. Does it give away something private about them, such as a health problem or a hard time at school? What seems relatable now may feel too personal to them later.

    If you're unsure, keep the more personal moments in a private family group or an offline album.

    💙 Explore Shift Your Perspective with Jay Shetty on Calm.

    Recent findings suggest that your past posts felt right at the time, and it’s okay if some show more than you’d share today. Scroll back through your posts for details like full names, school names, or locations.

    Delete the post, archive it, or move it to a private album if it feels too revealing.

    You're not the only one with a camera. Grandparents, co-parents, babysitters, and friends may post photos of your child too, usually out of love and pride. A conversation up front about family boundaries keeps everyone on the same page.

    leave full names and birth dates out of captions.

    skip location tags and recognizable landmarks in the background.

    use private groups or shared albums instead of public posts.

    check with you before posting anything.

    💙 Calm’s Kind Communication session can help you find the words for a warm, open conversation.

    Sharenting means posting about your child on social media, and the word blends "sharing" and "parenting." It covers anything from baby photos to regular updates as they grow up.

    Industry observers note that common sharenting examples include ultrasound pictures, birthday posts, funny quotes, and health or milestone updates. Even a photo that seems harmless can reveal more than you intended, like a club sign or a team jersey in the background.

    Many parents share to stay connected and celebrate their kids. Sharenting keeps faraway family members in the loop and connects you with other parents who get it. During hard stretches, it can help you feel less alone.

    The main risks of sharenting include a lasting digital footprint and exposed personal details. Photos can be saved, reshared, or collected by AI tools, which is why child safety groups encourage private accounts.

    That noted, many posts don’t lead to harm, and small habits like turning off location tags help lower the risks further.

    Recent findings suggest that sharenting shapes your child’s public image before they’re old enough to agree to it. Names, schools, and tagged locations can also reveal their routines to strangers, and a handful of details may be used for identity theft.

    If you keep personal moments offline now, your child has more room to shape their own image as they grow.

    There's no set age for when kids should have a say in what you post. Young kids may not fully understand what sharing means, so the decision starts with you. You can start asking as soon as they’re able to weigh in, and give their yes or no more weight as they grow.

    You can practice responsible sharenting with a mindful pause before you post. From there, check your privacy settings, and leave out personal details including names, schools, and locations. Ask for your child’s input once they’re old enough, and let family members know your boundaries.

    Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

    A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device.
    • We've been very happy with the reception so far.
    • It has been revealed that most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

    We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

    It has been revealed that most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of owners, not how much speech you generate.

    It has been revealed that getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

    We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

    According to recent reports, phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created newly introduced challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

    Sources indicate that phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the notable things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

    It has been revealed that it runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

    Recent findings suggest that the launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

    The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

    Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

    Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

    The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very fresh project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

    On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

    Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

    We built a upcoming inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

    Industry observers note that phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

    According to recent reports, it belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

    Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:.

    A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

    Sources indicate that the prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:.

    generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:.

    Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a fresh one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

    In a recent development, we also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

    Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

    In a recent development, phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

    Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

    According to recent reports, one line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly demonstrates where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

    Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software.
    • Industry observers note that image: Shutterstock.com.
    • According to recent reports, november’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid key security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

    Industry observers note that image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

    According to recent reports, november’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

    Industry observers note that this latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

    According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 indicates it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

    It has been revealed that several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

    Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

    According to recent reports, “I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”.

    Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A latest version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

    Industry observers note that adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

    Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

    It has been revealed that “Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”.

    It has been revealed that please don’t neglect to back up any crucial data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.
