    The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs.
    • According to recent reports, 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment.
    • Sources indicate that TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

    According to recent reports, 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

    Sources indicate that TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

    According to recent reports, the same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

    A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

    Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.

    Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

    Sources indicate that loRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

    It has been revealed that hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:.

    Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

    In a recent development, TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

    Sources indicate that first, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

    The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid demonstrates if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

    It has been revealed that O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

    Sources indicate that structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

    It has been revealed that the shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

    We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

    In a recent development, in the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

    Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

    It has been revealed that we add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

    Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

    According to recent reports, if we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

    Recent findings suggest that our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

    A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

    To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:.

    Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

    We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:.

    We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

    According to recent reports, the preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

    For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:.

    In a recent development, this container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

    The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

    Sources indicate that we use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

    If you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

    If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

    The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

    If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:.

    Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso.

    We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

    We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

    Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object.

    The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

    We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

    Recent findings suggest that we keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

    In a recent development, it’s crucial to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

    We revision only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

    It has been revealed that the snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

    We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

    We then follow these steps within the training loop:.

    The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

    Sources indicate that for each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

    We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

    The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

    Recent findings suggest that flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

    The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It highlights the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

    We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:.

    Industry observers note that in the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

    For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

    According to recent reports, phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

    The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

    Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

    In a recent development, gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

    #22960. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1587 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens.
    • To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models.
    • Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

    To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

    Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

    JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

    LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

    Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

    Industry observers note that LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

    The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

    Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):.

    The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

    The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

    Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

    In a recent development, we compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

    All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

    Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

    In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

    The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

    LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

    The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

    According to recent reports, LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the newly introduced vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

    This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

    Industry observers note that tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

    Any-to-pkl-community will convert json, yaml, toml to pkl, so just need the render part.

    How to stop emotional flooding from disrupting your relationships

    📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The argument started with the dishes.
    • Sources indicate that this is emotional flooding, and it can happen to anyone.
    • Flooding tends to show up when you're close to someone and the stakes feel personal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

    The argument started with the dishes. Now you're saying something you know you’ll regret. Two minutes ago, you were mildly annoyed. Now your heart is pounding, and you can barely hear your partner over the noise in your own head.

    Sources indicate that this is emotional flooding, and it can happen to anyone. It isn’t a character flaw, and it doesn’t mean you're bad at relationships. When emotions run hot, the level-headed version of you can seem to vanish.

    Flooding tends to show up when you're close to someone and the stakes feel personal. Fortunately, if you spot the signs early, you can keep an argument from turning into a blowup. Ahead, we’ll explore the science behind emotional flooding and how to calm yourself when it hits.

    Industry observers note that emotional flooding is a state of overwhelm during a heated moment, usually a conflict. The term comes from John Gottman, PhD, who describes flooding as the point when you’re so overloaded that you can't take in latest information, solve the problem, or hear the person in front of you.

    Gottman and his colleague Robert Levenson studied couples at the University of Washington. As partners argued, they tracked physical signals like heart rate. Couples whose bodies indicated higher arousal during conflict tended to grow less satisfied with their relationship over the following years.

    It has been revealed that flooding feels different from person to person, so you may notice some of these signs but not others. Here's what to look for:.

    Racing heart: Your pulse climbs, and you feel your heartbeat in your chest or throat.

    Fast, shallow breathing: Your breaths come quick and tight, and a full inhale feels out of reach.

    Heat and tension: Your face flushes, and your jaw or shoulders tighten.

    Tunnel vision: Your thinking narrows, and the other person’s words get hard to follow.

    Urge to fight or flee: You want to raise your voice or leave, and it feels difficult to hold back.

    Numbness or blankness: Your thoughts freeze, and you feel disconnected from the conversation.

    Emotional flooding involves the amygdala, the part of your brain built to detect danger and keep you safe. When it senses a threat, it triggers the stress response and releases a surge of hormones that put your body on high alert. Adrenaline and norepinephrine speed up your heart rate and pull your focus toward the threat. That narrowed focus is part of why listening gets so hard.

    In an everyday disagreement, there’s usually no physical danger, but your brain can still treat a raised voice or a difference of opinion as a threat, setting off the same alarm and the same rush of anger.

    In close relationships, flooding may get extra fuel. Arguments can touch things that matter deeply to you, like feeling respected or safe. Old wounds and fear of where the fight might lead can pile on top of the present moment.

    In a recent development, A note on relationships that don’t feel safe: This article is about everyday arguments, not abuse. If a raised voice or a pattern of control leaves you afraid of your partner, that fear isn’t a false alarm. Self-soothing isn’t the tool for this, and your safety comes first. You can reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline any time at 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788.

    You can't always stop flooding before it starts, but you can help your body calm down once you realize it’s happening. Then, when you feel settled enough to think clearly again, you can gently return to the conversation. The tips below follow that order: calm your body first, then come back and repair. Try the ones that fit the moment, and skip any that don’t feel right for you.

    In a recent development, the moment you notice your heart racing or your thoughts scrambling, tell yourself “this is flooding.” Naming it reminds you that the feeling is physical and temporary. That bit of awareness gives you room to choose your next move instead of reacting on autopilot.

    💙 Try the Full Sensory Awareness meditation on the Calm app.

    A longer exhale engages your parasympathetic nervous system, the part of your nervous system that helps you rest and settle down.

    In one study, people who practiced cyclic sighing (also known as the physiological sigh), a breathing pattern of two quick inhales and one long exhale, reported bigger mood improvements than those who practiced mindfulness meditation.

    If breathing exercises feel uncomfortable, skip ahead to the next tip.

    💙 Press play on the Breathe to Calm Down session on Calm.

    When you're flooded, stepping away can help you collect yourself before you talk things through. Tell your partner you need a break and that you’ll come back, so they don’t feel abandoned mid-conflict.

    Recent findings suggest that according to Gottman's research, it can take at least 20 minutes for your body to calm back down, so give yourself enough time. If you can’t leave the room, even a few minutes of silence can help.

    According to recent reports, your body often responds to physical cues faster than logic. Use your time-out to splash cold water on your face or step outside for a few minutes of fresh air. Either one can help slow your heart rate.

    💙 If anger is running hot, listen to Calm’s Investigating Anger session.

    Recent findings suggest that flooding releases stress hormones that prepare your body for action. A brisk walk, or any gentle movement that suits you, gives that energy somewhere to go instead of letting it build.

    Sources indicate that 💙 Explore Dr. Eric López's Walk Away Stress series on Calm.

    It has been revealed that once it feels calmer, return to your partner. You don't have to solve everything right away. A short repair can open the door to trying again.

    Industry observers note that try: “I got overwhelmed earlier. Can we try again?”.

    Gottman’s work suggests that how couples repair after conflict is a key predictor of long-term satisfaction, often more telling than how often they fight.

    💙 Learn how couples meditation can strengthen your relationship.

    Emotional flooding is feeling so overwhelmed during a conflict or another intense moment that you can’t think clearly or listen. The term comes from psychologist John Gottman's research on couples.

    In a recent development, A common example of emotional flooding is a tense meeting with your boss, when your heart starts pounding and your mind goes blank. It can also happen at home, like when a conversation with a family member or partner escalates.

    💙 Check out how to deal with a conflict at work.

    Emotional flooding is a surge of intense emotion in a specific moment, while emotional dysregulation is ongoing difficulty managing emotions across a range of situations. Flooding can be one sign of dysregulation, but if it happens now and then, that doesn’t necessarily mean you have a pattern of dysregulation.

    Emotional flooding can be more common and more intense for people with ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder). Studies show that trouble managing emotions is a core part of ADHD in adults. With ADHD, you may flood more often or take longer to calm down.

    If flooding feels constant or unmanageable, a doctor can help you figure out what’s behind it.

    💙 Learn what ADHD shutdown is and how to manage it.

    Industry observers note that you can stop being emotionally flooded by giving your body time to settle before you continue the conversation. Take a break of at least 20 minutes, and try long exhales, cold water on your face, or a brisk walk. When you feel more grounded, give the conversation another try.

    Industry observers note that mindfulness can help with emotional flooding because it trains you to notice early signs, such as a racing heart or a tight jaw, before they build. Over time, that gives you a chance to pause instead of react in hard moments.

    Try to practice mindfulness when you’re calm, with short breathing exercises or guided meditation, so the skill is there when you need it.

    It has been revealed that mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

    • Recent findings suggest that llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

    During the 3.5 years since its inception, the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work. We expect this trend to continue as local AI and privacy become increasingly important in our everyday lives. Every new integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount.

    Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

    The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:.

    Industry observers note that we are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-consumers. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

    According to recent reports, the project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

    According to recent reports, to reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

    The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

    A complete list of the presently implemented backends can be found here.

    We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Presently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

    Recent findings suggest that the llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

    #22953. Industry News: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1175 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail.
    • A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y.
    • Recent findings suggest that developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

    A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

    Recent findings suggest that developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

    The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

    People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

    We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

    For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

    Industry observers note that A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

    A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:.

    In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

    According to recent reports, to validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

    We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

    Sources indicate that across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

    A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

    We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

    A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

    Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to customers’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

    Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench at the moment covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

    We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

    Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run.
    • Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's.
    • The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

    Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

    The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:.

    Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent.

    The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise aims include monthly credits for compute and inference.

    It has been revealed that on OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

    Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

    Recent findings suggest that the best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

    Recent findings suggest that openRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million consumers, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

    OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

    According to recent reports, when a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the upcoming routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

    In a recent development, before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:.

    It has been revealed that routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

    In a recent development, pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

    In a recent development, image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

    In a recent development, on model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two fresh tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:.

    Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:.

    In a recent development, in your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

    Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

    Recent findings suggest that this is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:.

    #22947. Industry News: 101 fun questions for your kids to laugh, talk, and connect

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2773 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Calm ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: 101 fun questions for your kids to laugh, talk, and connect

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Have you ever asked your child what they did at school only to be told, “I don’t remember…”?
    • Many kids have a magical ability to give the least amount of detail possible when asked a direct question.
    • It has been revealed that the thing is, kids actually do want to talk.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Have you ever asked your child what they did at school only to be told, “I don’t remember…”?

    Many kids have a magical ability to give the least amount of detail possible when asked a direct question. It’s almost like they’re professionally trained in the art of dodging conversation.

    It has been revealed that the thing is, kids actually do want to talk. You just have to ask the right questions: ones that spark their imagination, make them laugh, or invite them to share something meaningful on their terms.

    It has been revealed that so, meet them where they are. Instead of the same old, “How was your day?” (which, let’s be honest, will never yield a thrilling response), try questions that make them pause and think for a moment. This way, you’re not prying information out of them, you’re building a habit of open conversation, one fun question at a time.

    Ask them in the car, at bedtime, over breakfast, or whenever your kid is in a chatty mood. You might be surprised at what they share — and the hilarious, heartwarming, or even unexpectedly deep conversations that follow.

    Laughter is one of the easiest ways to connect with your child (and can boost your mental health too). These offbeat, ridiculous questions will get them giggling while giving you a glimpse into their wonderfully weird little minds.

    It has been revealed that would you rather have a banana for a nose or popcorn for ears? Kids love absurd choices, and these “would you rather” questions are a surefire way to spark hilarious debates.

    Would you rather have spaghetti for hair or marshmallows for fingers?

    Would you rather live in a house made of chocolate or a castle made of cheese?

    Would you rather always talk in rhymes or only be able to whisper?

    Would you rather ride a roller coaster that never ends or a Ferris wheel that goes super fast?

    Would you rather have a pet dragon or a pet unicorn?

    Ever wonder what your backpack thinks about your daily routine? These questions help kids think outside the box — and maybe appreciate their favorite objects a little more.

    If your socks could talk, what would they say about your feet?

    If your toothbrush had feelings, how would it feel about its job?

    If your toys threw a party while you were sleeping, what would they do?

    According to recent reports, the best questions to ask kids are open-ended, playful, and relevant to their world. Instead of asking, “Did you have a good day?”—which almost always leads to a dead-end answer—try something that sparks their imagination or invites storytelling, like “What was the funniest thing that happened today?” or “If you could switch places with your teacher for a day, what would you do?” Kids are much more likely to engage when a question feels fun, unexpected, and free of pressure.

    According to recent reports, kids love absurdity, so the weirder and wackier the question, the better. Offbeat questions tap into their creativity, making conversation feel more like a game than a chore.

    According to recent reports, silly questions are also a great way to bond, especially when you play along. If your kid tells you they’d rather ride a roller coaster that never stops over a Ferris wheel that goes super fast, ask why and join in the fun by sharing your own ridiculous answer.

    Laughter is a powerful connector, and sometimes the most unexpected conversations start with a totally goofy question.

    For 6-year-olds, short questions about things they can picture work best. Silly choices and pretend play go over well. Try “What would you name a pet cloud?” or “If your stuffed animals had jobs, what would they be?” Many of the funny questions above fit this age, especially the “would you rather” and “If your stuff could talk” lists. Ask one question at a time, since young kids can lose the thread when you ask two at once.

    Which question to ask depends on what you want from the chat. If you want laughs, pick a “would you rather” or other funny question. If you want to know your child better, choose from the get-to-know list. For big feelings, try the emotional expression questions. When you’re not sure, start silly to help them relax, then move to a deeper one.

    It has been revealed that kids spend a lot of their day being told what to do—sit still, follow directions, finish their homework—so having a space where they get to lead the conversation is powerful. Asking fun and engaging questions gives them a chance to express themselves, think creatively, and feel heard without any right or wrong answers. It also helps build communication skills, emotional intelligence, and a sense of connection with you.

    Recent findings suggest that beyond that, these questions create opportunities for everyday bonding. A quick chat in the car or during dinner can turn into a meaningful moment of connection. The more kids feel like their thoughts and ideas are valued, the more likely they are to open up — not just about the silly stuff but about the big things, too.

    The key to getting good answers is making the conversation feel natural, not forced. If you ask a question and get a one-word response, don’t panic — sometimes kids just need a little extra space to warm up. Try following up with, “Tell me more!” or sharing your own answer first to get the ball rolling. If they see that you’re genuinely interested (and willing to be a little silly yourself), they’ll be more likely to engage.

    Also, be thoughtful about your timing. Some kids open up more when they’re relaxed—like at bedtime or when you’re doing an activity together—while others chat more when they’re distracted, like in the car. If they’re tired, hungry, or mid-screen time, you might not get much out of them. But if you catch them in the right moment, you might just unlock a goldmine of thoughts, ideas, and hilarious kid logic.

    Sources indicate that the best time to ask kids questions is when they’re naturally more open to conversation — when they feel safe, relaxed, and not pressured to respond. For some kids, that’s during bedtime, when they’re winding down and their thoughts start to flow. For others, it’s in the car, when there’s no pressure for eye contact and they can talk freely. Meal times, walks, or even while playing with Legos can also be great moments to slip in a fun question.

    Trying to force deep conversation right after school when their brain is fried or when they’re engrossed in a game or show usually won’t work. Instead, look for organic, low-pressure moments when chatting feels easy. And remember, it’s not about when you ask, it’s about showing up consistently so that when they are ready to talk, they know you’ll be there to listen.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In conventional session-based authentication, the server manages session information for each authenticated user.
    • Each request carries an unique identifier or token (such as a signed, self-contained JWT) that the server validates before granting access.
    • APIs are constant targets for unauthorized access and exposure of sensitive information.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In conventional session-based authentication, the server manages session information for each authenticated user. Stateless authentication, however, involves each request carrying the information needed to authenticate a user. This means the server doesn’t need to maintain previous request or session data.

    Each request carries an unique identifier or token (such as a signed, self-contained JWT) that the server validates before granting access. This process is more independent and can be easily adopted for distributed applications. It is also well suited for REST APIs, where JWTs enable stateless authentication without requiring server-side session storage.

    APIs are constant targets for unauthorized access and exposure of sensitive information. Securing them requires authentication, authorization, and token validation at every endpoint. This ensures that only authorized users can create, enhancement, or delete resources.

    It has been revealed that in OAuth2 protocol, first the Resource Owner grants permission to the Client, which then requests authorized access from the Auth Server. Once approved, the Authorization Server complications JWT signature as an access token, which the Client sends to the Resource Server (API).

    This allows the server to independently authenticate each request without relying on previous session data. JwtAuthenticationConverter checks the claims in JWT and maps them to a collection of GrantedAuthority objects. For that particular request, a stateless Authentication object is placed in the SecurityContext.

    Spring Security has built-in support for stateless authentication. SecurityFilterChain is used to configure security rules and disable any server-side HTTP sessions (SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS). JWT authentication components validate tokens for incoming requests. In simple steps, this can be implemented as follows:.

    It has been revealed that once the security configuration is ready, JWTs can handle authentication for incoming HTTP requests. The client sends the access token in the Authorization header (Authorization: Bearer ), and Spring Security validates it.

    If the token is valid (and has not expired yet), the request is processed. If the token is invalid, the API throws an authentication error.

    Below is a simple implementation of how to configure JWT authentication in Spring Security:.

    This keeps the authentication stateless while allowing Spring Security to verify each incoming request with JWT.

    It has been revealed that APIs are the gateways between applications and protected data, which is why securing them is essential. Otherwise, anyone with an API endpoint could potentially access sensitive data. This tutorial shows how to secure a Spring Boot API with OAuth2 and JWTs, so the backend validates tokens without ever touching the user credentials itself. OAuth2 and JWTs work together: OAuth2 manages delegated access and JWTs carry the verified identity and access claims.

    Industry observers note that if you’re building a Spring Boot API and have been putting off the security aspects, this tutorial is a good starting point. It is particularly relevant to Kotlin developers with basic Spring Security knowledge who want to implement stateless authentication in REST APIs.     Empathy vs compassion: the difference (with real-life examples)

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr.
    • Industry observers note that understanding and connecting with another person—either through empathy or compassion—facilitates more meaningful interactions and relationships.
    • Knowing the differences between empathy and compassion can help us approach others and what they’re going through with understanding and kindness.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

    Industry observers note that understanding and connecting with another person—either through empathy or compassion—facilitates more meaningful interactions and relationships. Whether it’s a friend going through a tough time or a family member facing a challenge, how we connect with them can significantly impact the support we offer.

    Knowing the differences between empathy and compassion can help us approach others and what they’re going through with understanding and kindness.

    Compassion is concern for another person's well-being and happiness, and a genuine urge to help alleviate their suffering. Compassion isn’t just a fleeting emotion — it’s a lasting state, a readiness to extend a helping hand whenever possible. (For the full definition, here’s our guide to what compassion is.).

    Empathy is the capability to tune into someone else’s emotions and to feel what they’re feeling. Empathy means genuinely trying to understand another person’s feelings and perspective.

    💙 Sharpen your listening skills and make others truly feel heard with Jay Shetty in this Supportive Listening meditation.

    It has been revealed that while both empathy and compassion are avenues to connect with others, their core essence and impact are different. While empathy allows for emotional understanding, compassion takes it further by driving action. It's about moving from feeling to doing, from emotional resonance to proactive kindness.

    Through this understanding, we can see the value of cultivating empathy and practicing compassion in our daily actions, which not only enrich our relationships but positively impact our communities, too.

    Industry observers note that empathy steers emotional connection. It's about feeling the same emotions that another person is experiencing and aligning emotionally because of that similarity. On the other hand, compassion drives us towards a deep understanding of another's distress, coupled with a desire to make them feel better. It's not just about feeling, it’s about understanding and taking action.

    Empathy is rooted in deeply feeling what another person is going through and mirroring their emotional state. Compassion is about acknowledging what the other people are going through instead of feeling the emotion yourself.

    Recent findings suggest that empathy often revolves around an inward reflection that allows us to feel the emotions that another person is experiencing. Compassion propels us outward and encourages acting on the feeling to help alleviate someone else’s discomfort.

    Sources indicate that empathy primarily consists of feeling the emotional state of another, while compassion is action-oriented. Compassion prompts us to take steps to ease another's suffering, no matter how small.

    Industry observers note that empathy, although a profound feeling, can be more of a momentary emotional connection that is often fleeting once the shared emotion dissipates. Compassion, on the other hand, reflects a long-term commitment to assisting others and a consistent readiness to help.

    Sources indicate that 💙 Learn more about Empathy vs. Compassion with this Daily Jay session.

    You usually won’t choose between them in the moment. They tend to show up together. Here’s how each one can look in the same situation.

    Sources indicate that empathy is feeling with someone. Compassion is taking a step to help. You won’t usually pick one in the moment, since feeling with someone is often what leads you to help.

    Empathy and compassion are ways to connect with others, but they play different roles. Empathy is about feeling the same emotions that someone else is feeling. For example, if a friend is sad, you feel sad along with them. Compassion takes empathy a step further. It’s about recognizing someone’s distress and wanting to help alleviate it. So, when you see someone in trouble, not only do you understand their problem, but you also want to help sort it out. Compassion motivates us to act and make a positive difference, while empathy encourages us to feel and relate.

    According to recent reports, both empathy and compassion are valuable in building meaningful relationships. Empathy helps in understanding other people’s emotions and creating bonds. Compassion, however, not only understands but also propels us to take action to help. It’s about moving from feeling to doing something helpful. Empathy can be a stepping stone to compassion, leading us from feeling to taking positive action.

    Being empathetic and compassionate is like having a superpower for creating solid and supportive relationships. Empathy allows you to understand others' feelings, while compassion motivates you to take action to help. It’s a blend that encourages understanding while making a positive impact in others’ lives. Empathy and compassion go hand in hand, enhancing our connections with others and making our social interactions more meaningful and enriching.

    According to recent reports, empathetic and compassionate leadership both aim to create a supportive work environment, but they do so in slightly different ways. Empathetic leadership is about understanding employees' emotions and perspectives and creating an environment where people feel heard and understood. Compassionate leadership, on the other hand, not only understands but takes action to support and help employees, recognizing the challenges and actively working to provide support or solutions. Compassionate leadership often brings a more supportive and caring work culture, benefiting both employees and the organization.
