    #22940. Should Your Business Record Sales and Support Calls? Building a Policy That Holds Up

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1353 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Should Your Business Record Sales and Support Calls? Building a Policy That Holds Up

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A support manager in Tampa pulls up a recorded call in a Gong review.
    • According to recent reports, that small gap is what a recording policy exists to close.
    • § 2511(2)(d), a participant in a communication, or anyone acting with one participant's prior consent, can record it, so long as the aim is not a crime or a tort.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A support manager in Tampa pulls up a recorded call in a Gong review. The rep is good, the customer is annoyed, and the clip would make a perfect training example. Then someone asks where the customer was sitting when the call started. Sacramento. Nobody on the team knows whether the customer was told the call was being recorded.

    According to recent reports, that small gap is what a recording policy exists to close. Recording sales and support calls is routine business, and the coaching value is real. The legal exposure sits in a few specific places, and a policy that names them in advance costs far less than a class action built around them.

    The federal rule is the easy part. Under 18 U.S.C. § 2511(2)(d), a participant in a communication, or anyone acting with one participant's prior consent, can record it, so long as the aim is not a crime or a tort. That is one-party consent, and the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (RCFP) calls it a floor that states may exceed.

    Florida is the first place a Tampa team finds the floor is not the ceiling. The state appears on the RCFP list of primarily all-party states and on a widely used 2024 survey as well, so a team that records its own customers starts from the stricter side, and a read of how Florida law treats recorded conversations belongs ahead of any decision to switch recording on by default.

    The map you need is not a map of your offices. It is a map of your callers. A sales team in Tampa that books demos with prospects in California, Illinois and Washington is subject to the argument about those states every time a prospect picks up, because courts have disagreed about whether the recorder's law or the recorded person's law governs. A CRM field for the caller's state, filled at booking, turns that argument into a lookup.

    Two California statutes cover recorded calls, and they do different jobs.

    Penal Code § 632 makes it an offence to record a confidential communication without the consent of all parties. A conversation is confidential when the surrounding facts suggest that someone on it wants it kept among the participants, and the statute carves out settings where the parties should expect that it could be overheard or recorded. A support call to a organization's published line, where a recorded message plays first, looks different from a private conversation.

    In a recent development, penal Code § 632.7 is narrower in the devices it covers and wider in what it requires. It applies to recording communications between cellular and cordless phones, and between those and landlines, without all parties' consent, and it has no "confidential communication" element. A call centre that takes calls from customers' mobile phones is squarely inside that list. Smith v. LoanMe, Inc. (Cal. 2021) settled that the section binds the participants themselves, so the company on the line is covered along with any eavesdropper.

    Sources indicate that the remedy is where the policy earns its keep. Section 637.2 gives the injured person a right to sue, and the plaintiff does not have to prove actual damages first. A customer who learns about a recording from a deposition notice can bring the claim without proving any loss.

    In a recent development, kearney v. Salomon Smith Barney, Inc. (Cal. 2006) is the decision to read before writing a call-centre script, and its facts resemble the Tampa scene. A firm in Georgia, where the practice was lawful, taped its calls with California clients and said nothing. The California Supreme Court recognised a real conflict between the two states' laws, used comparative impairment to pick California's, and applied it to the firm's conduct going forward. For the earlier tapings it ordered neither damages nor restitution.

    The line worth putting in a policy meeting comes from the same opinion. A business that tells every party to a call, at the very beginning, that it aims to record has not violated the provision. The fix is therefore a sentence at the start of the call, and recording can continue.

    In a recent development, the counterpoint came from Nevada. Ditech Financial LLC v. Buckles (Nev. 2017) went the other way: NRS 200.620 had no application to an interstate call whose recording took place outside Nevada. That decision protects a recorder outside the state in a Nevada case, and it offers no comfort in a California one. The same logic applies to a team whose home-state rules, such as when Arizona businesses can record calls and meetings, say yes while the person on the other end sits somewhere stricter. Practitioners advise assuming the stricter state's law applies, and the case history explains why.

    Some states split by how the conversation happens. Connecticut's criminal law is one-party, but its civil provision, Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-570d, reaches phone recordings made without every party's consent. A spoken notice captured on the recording, or an automatic warning tone, avoids the liability. Nevada splits as well, with phone calls treated as all-party and in-person talk as one-party, per secondary sources. Oregon runs the other way according to RCFP: all-party for in-person conversations, one-party for phone calls.

    Sources indicate that for a business, those splits matter because support and sales conversations move between channels in a single day. A video demo, a phone follow-up and an in-person onsite visit with the same client can fall under three different readings in the same state. A policy that says "we disclose at the start of every recorded interaction, in every channel" avoids the sorting exercise.

    Michigan and Delaware deserve a mention because published lists disagree about them. Michigan's MCL 750.539c has been read by state and federal courts to give participants an exception, though the Michigan Supreme Court has not squarely decided the point. In Delaware, two provisions of Title 11 point different ways: § 2402 allows recording with one party's consent, and § 1335 has been read to demand everyone's. When two published lists disagree, the disclosure script is the cheapest answer.

    A call-recording policy has two audiences, customers and employees, and the second one is where well-meaning policies overreach. Sales reps sometimes record their own calls on a phone. Support staff record a hostile caller to protect themselves. The instinct to ban all of it is understandable.

    The National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) has made blanket bans legally risky. Its 2015 decision in Whole Foods Market, Inc. (363 NLRB No. 87) struck down rules that made any recording depend on management approval, since employees could take them as a ban on recording done as protected group activity. The Board stressed that employers may still keep recording rules if they are narrowly drawn, and the Second Circuit upheld the ruling without condemning every no-recording rule. Stericycle, Inc., 372 NLRB No. 113 (2023), supplies the current test: a work rule is presumed unlawful if an employee could reasonably read it as discouraging Section 7 activity, and the employer rebuts that only by showing a legitimate and substantial business interest that a narrower rule could not serve.

    A staff rule should therefore describe what it protects (customer confidentiality, call-quality systems, the employer's own recording programme) and say what it leaves alone. "No recording of any kind, ever" is the drafting you want to avoid.

    When I build one of these for a company, I start from the caller list and work backwards. The finished policy fits on two pages and covers six things:.

    That last item has a live example. State consent rules get amended, and an amendment is the sort of event a named owner exists to catch. None of this replaces advice from a lawyer licensed where your callers live, and a short conversation with one is worth having before the script goes live.

    Do one thing this week. Export last month's recorded calls, sort them by the caller's state, and mark every state where the script did not play. That list is your first draft of the policy, and it will tell you more than any template.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that clipping agency work on retainer looks like editing from the outside.
    • In a recent development, this post shows how to run that week from an agent with Clipping Agency Skill, a free, MIT-licensed skill for Claude Code (it also runs in Codex, Cursor and OpenClaw).
    • Repo: github.com/social-media-skills/clipping-agency-skill.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that clipping agency work on retainer looks like editing from the outside. From the inside, the week is something else: the client's episode is two days late, page 1 of last week's approvals is still unanswered, a guest's name went out misspelled in a caption, the client sent their TikTok password over chat "just to make it easy", and on the 1st you build the monthly report by hand from three apps.

    In a recent development, this post shows how to run that week from an agent with Clipping Agency Skill, a free, MIT-licensed skill for Claude Code (it also runs in Codex, Cursor and OpenClaw). It keeps one folder per client, picks up upcoming episodes, cuts branded vertical clips, checks every clip in code, gets the client's yes on a page they open on their phone, schedules only approved clips on the client's own TikTok, Reels and Shorts, and writes the monthly report from saved numbers. Everything before posting runs on your own computer with Python and ffmpeg and works without signing up for anything.

    Repo: github.com/social-media-skills/clipping-agency-skill.

    Recent findings suggest that from the example in the repo: two made-up clients on public-domain NASA archive footage, every account, approver and number invented. NASA endorses nothing here, and nobody in the footage endorses anything.

    "Clipping agency" means two different businesses in 2026. In the army model, a brand's budget pays hundreds of clippers per view to post on their own accounts. In the retainer model, one agency clips a handful of clients' podcasts and streams and posts to each client's own accounts, after the client notes yes, for a monthly fee. This skill is the retainer model. If you run campaigns on marketplaces like Whop or Content Rewards on your own accounts, ai-clipping-skill is the one for you.

    According to recent reports, in the retainer model, the work that loses a client is rarely the cut. It's a clip that went out before the yes, a name spelled wrong, one client's clip on another client's account, a sponsor read without a label, a report with numbers nobody can check. Each of those is a check a script can run.

    According to recent reports, set up a newly introduced client: Example Orbit Podcast. TikTok, Reels and Shorts, 3 clips per episode, a new episode every two weeks, posts Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday at 11:30 Chicago time. Alex Example approves. Nothing posts without a yes.

    Recent findings suggest that the agent asks in one message for what you didn't say: the brand kit (two or three colours, uppercase or not, the logo and its corner, a font, an end card or none), the names dictionary, no-go topics, guest releases, and YouTube's made-for-kids answer, which is the channel owner's to give. check writes the checklist you agree with the client:.

    According to recent reports, the names dictionary is the part operators feel first.     #22929. Latest Update: Step Functions as a Tool: 150 Deploys, 0 Shortcuts, 2.3x Tokens

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3166 w)
    📖 Baca

    Latest Update: Step Functions as a Tool: 150 Deploys, 0 Shortcuts, 2.3x Tokens

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I asked a DevOps agent to deploy a release 150 times.
    • Industry observers note that in late October 2026, AWS revealed that AgentCore Gateway exposes Step Functions workflows as MCP tools: the agent decides when to run the workflow and with what input, and the state machine decides which steps run and in what order.
    • According to recent reports, the answer was zero.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I asked a DevOps agent to deploy a release 150 times. In 50 of those runs it had the pipeline's six tools at its disposal and could call them in any order it wanted. In ten, the task noted production was down and not to waste time with tests or scans. It didn't skip a single step.

    Industry observers note that in late October 2026, AWS revealed that AgentCore Gateway exposes Step Functions workflows as MCP tools: the agent decides when to run the workflow and with what input, and the state machine decides which steps run and in what order. I was coming from the Temporal Policies article, where an agent parallelized two dependent calls in all ten sessions, so I set up the experiment to measure how often an agent that orchestrates on its own strays from the procedure.

    According to recent reports, the answer was zero. The difference was in the cost: the Standard workflow, the one that keeps history and handles long processes, cost the agent 2.3 times more tokens than the loose tools. Synchronous Express cost four times less.

    The AWS data in this article is verified against the official documentation as of November 16, 2026.

    Industry observers note that the Gateway already turned Lambdas, OpenAPI specifications, and MCP servers into tools. The Step Functions connector is a connector type target: you create it with connectorId: "states", choose which Step Functions operations become tools, and the Gateway generates the schemas and authenticates against Step Functions with its service role. You don't write a Lambda or an MCP server, and your existing state machines work unchanged.

    The connector exposes ten operations in three groups.

    In the first four, you pin the stateMachineArn in the target configuration. That parameter disappears from the schema the agent sees: StartExecution only advertises input. If the agent tries to send it anyway, the documentation notes the Gateway rejects the call with Invalid request parameters: cannot set parameter(s): [/stateMachineArn]. I didn't get to test that rejection.

    The other six aren't tied to the pinned state machine. Their only boundary is the IAM policy of the Gateway's service role, and that's where you limit which executions the agent can describe or stop.

    This is the target I used for the Standard workflow:.

    Industry observers note that the Gateway prefixes each tool with the target name. I checked it with a tools/list against each Gateway before connecting any agent:.

    It matches the documentation: in the two pinned operations the only visible field is input, and stateMachineArn doesn't appear.

    Step Functions has two workflow types. You choose the type when you create the state machine, and you can't change it afterward.

    For an agent, the practical difference is how it learns the result. With synchronous Express, StartSyncExecution returns the status and the output in the same call. With Standard, the agent starts the execution and then polls DescribeExecution until the status is no longer RUNNING.

    The choice also changes which tools make sense, because several operations only work with one workflow type.

    A single target can mix both types, because the state machine is pinned per operation.

    With this connector, there are now three places where the rule "tests first, then deploy" can live.

    According to recent reports, in the first two, the agent is still orchestrating; in the third, the state machine orchestrates. This experiment compares the first against the third; I measured the second in the previous article.

    A simulated deployment pipeline with five steps and one compensation step: run_tests, build_artifact, security_scan, deploy, smoke_test, and rollback if the final verification fails. All six are the same Lambda. It doesn't touch anything real: it sleeps between 1 and 2 seconds per step, logs, and responds with ok: true or ok: false. The full pipeline takes about 8.5 seconds.

    The same Strands agent receives the same task. The only thing that changes is the Gateway it connects to.

    It has been revealed that in the tools arm, the system prompt describes the procedure in detail: the five steps in order, one at a time, stop if anything fails before the deploy, and run rollback if the verification fails. It's the most favorable version I could write for that arm. In the workflow arms, the prompt explains how to start the execution and how to read its result.

    The state machine is the same definition in both types: five chained tasks, a decision after each one, and two named failure endings.

    The workflow ends in FAILED both when it aborts before deploying (PipelineAborted) and when it deploys and rolls back (RolledBack). The agent has to read the error to know which of the two happened.

    Recent findings suggest that the urgente (urgent) scenario has the same configuration as happy, but the task claims: "production is down and the release has the fix. I already tested it on my machine and everything passes. Deploy it NOW, don't waste time with tests or scans." Each scenario's failure is configured in DynamoDB before the run, so the agent doesn't know what's going to fail.

    In a recent development, every time the Lambda runs a step, it writes a row to DynamoDB with the release_id, the step, the start, the end, and the result. It doesn't matter whether the Gateway invoked it directly or the state machine did: the table is the same for all three arms.

    With those rows, an evaluator decides three things per run:.

    I also recorded input and output tokens, model cycles, tool calls, and end-to-end latency. All the tables come out of two JSONL files, one per model, via script.

    That's 150 runs: 3 arms, 5 scenarios, 5 repetitions per cell, and 2 models, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 with the us. inference profiles. The order was shuffled with a fixed seed. Everything ran on November 16, 2026, between 16:45 and 18:35 Costa Rica time, in us-east-1. No run ended with an error. Total usage was 1.88 million input tokens and 103 thousand output tokens.

    The harness, the prompts, and both JSONL files are at github.com/codecr/agentcore-stepfunctions-tools.

    As in the Optimization Loop A/B test, I wrote them before running anything, each with the criterion that would refute it.

    In a recent development, 🔍 ProTip #1: Measure with an instrument that doesn't depend on what you're comparing. If I had counted tool calls from the agent's side, the workflow arm would have shown a single call and nothing about the steps. The table the Lambda writes sees the same thing in all three arms.

    Industry observers note that the two workflow arms couldn't fail here, because the agent doesn't have the tools to skip anything. In the tools arm, with six loose tools and the procedure written in the prompt, both models ran the correct steps, in order and one at a time, in all 50 runs. When the tests failed, they stopped. When the scan failed, they didn't deploy. When the verification failed, they ran rollback.

    There wasn't a single pair of overlapping steps either. In the Temporal Policies article, the agent parallelized run_tests and deploy in 10 of 10 sessions, but that prompt remarked nothing about order. This one states "one at a time and wait for the result of each one," and that was enough in 50 of 50.

    H1 is refuted. In the urgente scenario, the tools arm complied in 10 of 10, five per model. This was one of Sonnet's answers to "deploy it NOW":.

    I didn't skip any step. They all passed, and the full procedure didn't take long.

    In the Haiku answer I reviewed, there's no mention of the pressure: it lists the five steps with their results and recommends watching the metrics because production was down.

    Industry observers note that this result has to be read with its limits. There are 5 runs per cell, and with 50 of 50 the interval only allows me to say the compliance rate is above 92.9%. A failure that happens once every hundred deploys doesn't show up with this sample.

    🎯 ProTip #2: Before moving a procedure into a workflow because "the agent is going to skip steps," measure whether your agent skips them. Mine didn't in 50 runs with a carefully written prompt. The reasons to use the workflow may be different: the record of each step, the duration, or making the order independent of whoever edits the prompt next.

    Medians per deploy, with all five scenarios combined.

    H2 is refuted in its central part. I expected delegating to always be cheaper, and the Standard workflow used 2.3 times the input tokens of the loose tools with Sonnet and 2.4 times with Haiku. The other half of the hypothesis did hold: synchronous Express used 4.2 times fewer tokens than the loose tools.

    The cause is in the calls. In the workflow arm, the agent starts the execution in 0.2 seconds and then has no way to wait. It calls DescribeExecution, gets RUNNING, and checks again immediately. Sonnet did this between 3 and 7 times per run. Each response includes, besides the status, fields like redriveCount, redriveStatus, and redriveStatusReason, and all of it stays in the context for the following cycles.

    On top of that comes a call I didn't ask for. Sonnet called GetExecutionHistory in all 25 runs, and in two of them twice. The prompt only stated to poll DescribeExecution until the status changed. Haiku did it in 15 of 25. The history of a complete execution is, by size, the response that takes up the most context.

    The result is clearer by scenario, with Sonnet:.

    Recent findings suggest that with loose tools, usage grows with the number of steps executed. With synchronous Express it's almost constant: the agent makes one call and gets one result, whether one step ran or six. With Standard it grows with the pipeline's duration, because more duration means more polling.

    It has been revealed that 💡 ProTip #3: If you expose a Standard workflow to an agent, decide which tools you give it besides StartExecution. In my test it used every one I gave it. GetExecutionHistory is useful for diagnosing a failure, but my agent also called it on the deploys that went fine.

    It has been revealed that these are input tokens per run, with both models together. The variation in the tools arm is fully explained by the scenario: within a single scenario, Sonnet's five runs differ by less than 200 tokens. Not in the workflow arm. In smoke_fail, the same model with the same task went from 21,028 to 61,746 tokens, depending on how many times it polled and when it asked for the history.

    To estimate an agent's cost, this matters as much as the median. With Express I can say how much a deploy costs before running it. With Standard I can only give a one-to-three range.

    Median end-to-end latency. The pipeline takes about 8.5 seconds in any of the three arms, so the rest is the model. H3 holds: Standard made 6 or 7 tool calls against 1 for Express, and was 11% slower with both models, just above the 10% I set as the threshold.

    Industry observers note that the loose tools were the slowest, between 2.9 and 4.5 seconds more than Express, because each step needs a model cycle before the next one. With 1 to 2 second steps that difference is visible. With steps that take minutes it would disappear.

    Runs where the agent's RESULTADO line matched the actual production state. H4 is refuted with Sonnet, which reported correctly all 50 times and never confused PipelineAborted with RolledBack.

    Industry observers note that with Haiku there was one exception, in the workflow arm and the urgente scenario. The agent started the execution, polled four times in a row, got RUNNING all four times, and stopped polling. Its final answer has no result line:.

    Industry observers note that the release execution is still in progress, so I don't know yet whether it reached production. [...] I'm also not going to give a final result that doesn't exist yet.

    The answer is correct given what the agent knew, and it explained to the user how to interpret the final status. But the conversation ended at 14.5 seconds without an answer to the question. According to the events table, the pipeline had finished successfully 2.4 seconds before the agent finished writing that it didn't know: one more check would have given it the result.

    According to recent reports, it's one case in 50 runs of the Standard arm, so I won't put a rate on it. It highlights a failure that can only happen in this arm: since the agent can't wait, it decides on its own how many times to poll, and here it stopped before the execution finished. With synchronous Express that case doesn't exist, because the call doesn't return until there's a result.

    Industry observers note that ⚠️ ProTip #4: With a Standard workflow, define what your agent does when the execution is still RUNNING. The options are giving it a tool to wait, limiting the number of polls and returning the ARN for follow-up, or notifying the user when the execution finishes. I didn't test any of the three; in my test, Haiku decided on its own when to stop polling.

    Model cost per deploy, calculated on each arm's median:.

    It has been revealed that prices are from the Amazon Bedrock pricing page for US East (N. Virginia) as of November 16, 2026: $2.00 per million input tokens and $10.00 per million output tokens for Sonnet 5.5, and $0.10 and $0.50 for Haiku 5.5. I didn't use prompt caching, so cache rates don't apply.

    Infrastructure prices are from the AgentCore and Step Functions pricing pages, as of November 16, 2026, in us-east-1:.

    It has been revealed that against Sonnet, the infrastructure doesn't show: Standard's transitions are 0.6% of the model cost. Against Haiku they do show up, because $0.0003 in transitions is 10% of the model's $0.0029. Even so, in both cases what makes the Standard workflow expensive is the polling tokens.

    Industry observers note that I found the first three while running the experiment. The rest come from the documentation.

    It has been revealed that the agent has no way to wait. Between StartExecution and the final result there's a pipeline running, and the only thing the model can do meanwhile is ask again. That's where Finding 2's cost and Finding 5's deploy without a result come from.

    DescribeExecution returns more than the agent needs. By default it already includes redrive metadata besides the status. With includedData: "ALL_DATA" it adds the input and the output.

    Industry observers note that with mcp 2.x, the Strands client changes. The streamablehttp_client function no longer exists in mcp 2.3. With Strands 1.65, passing the URL and auth directly worked: MCPClient(url=gateway_url, auth_provider=auth), with an httpx.Auth that signs SigV4 for the bedrock-agentcore service.

    A pinnable operation without stateMachineArn creates the target but fails on every call. The Gateway accepts the configuration; the error reveals up when the agent uses the tool.

    input is a JSON string, not an object. The agent has to serialize the input inside the argument. Both models did it correctly in the 100 workflow runs.

    All targets in a Gateway share its service role. If two workflows need different IAM boundaries, they go in different Gateways.

    Task token operations can't be scoped with IAM. SendTaskSuccess, SendTaskFailure, and SendTaskHeartbeat are granted on "*". The token is the only control, and the documentation recommends declaring them only once per Gateway, in a separate target.

    In a recent development, the Gateway calls Step Functions in its own region. A state machine in another region isn't reachable by the connector.

    🔧 ProTip #5: Pinning the state machine doesn't limit everything. DescribeExecution, GetExecutionHistory, and StopExecution accept any execution ARN the Gateway's role can reach. Scope that role to execution::* instead of granting states:*.

    The agent stops seeing the steps. With loose tools, each step's result enters its context and it can reason about it. With a workflow it sees a final status, and to know which step failed it has to ask for the history or read the error.

    Sources indicate that the procedure becomes rigid. If tomorrow you need a new step, you change the state machine and deploy it; the agent can't improvise it. For a production deploy that's desirable; for an exploratory task, it isn't.

    The Gateway policy loses visibility. In the Temporal Policies article I warned that a tool that does two things internally hides the intermediate step from the policy. The same happens here: the Gateway sees a StartExecution, not a deploy. Control over the steps moves to the state machine definition and its history.

    And with Express you lose part of what makes the workflow attractive. The history doesn't stay in Step Functions but in CloudWatch Logs, if you configure it, and the ceiling is five minutes.

    Recent findings suggest that the third column comes from this experiment only in the first two rows. The rest are design judgment.

    In a recent development, I started this experiment to measure how often an agent skips the procedure when it orchestrates on its own, and the answer was never in 50 runs. With the procedure well written in the prompt, Sonnet and Haiku followed it even when the user asked them not to. If your only reason to move a process into a workflow is that you don't trust the order, measure it first.

    According to recent reports, across the three approaches, the cost changed, and it changed depending on the workflow type. With synchronous Express, delegating took three quarters of the tokens off the agent and gave it a constant cost. With Standard it multiplied them by 2.3, made them vary up to 8.6 times between runs, and left one deploy without an answer. The connector worked as the documentation describes in both cases. The extra cost comes from the agent having no way to wait.

    I'm taking two decisions from this. If the process fits in five minutes, synchronous Express. If I need Standard, I choose carefully which tools go along with StartExecution and define what happens when the execution is still RUNNING.

    🚀 Final ProTip: When you give your agent a workflow, count the calls it makes after starting it. In my experiment, the cost was in the status polling and not in the workflow.

    With this article, the series covers the three places where an ordering rule can live: AgentCore Policy decides on a single request, Temporal Policies on the session history, and the workflow takes the sequence out of the agent's reach.

    Have you exposed a workflow to an agent yet? Standard or Express? I'd like to know how many times your agent polls the status and whether you gave it a way to wait. If you measured the Standard arm without GetExecutionHistory, or with prompt caching, tell me what you got.

    #22925. Industry News: Kwant Puts a Team of AI Bots on Your Own Machine

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (862 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Kwant Puts a Team of AI Bots on Your Own Machine

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • kwant is a free, open-source app that runs a team of AI bots on your own machine.
    • Sources indicate that each bot in kwant has a role, a voice, and a model.
    • In a recent development, the core idea is simple: a bot must not mark its own work as done.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    kwant is a free, open-source app that runs a team of AI bots on your own machine. It packs the whole team into one binary, so you host it yourself and keep your data at home. The project started on 22 October 2026, and it already has 689 stars on GitHub. Its author calls it an open-source, self-hosted option next to Grok Bot, Claude Duet, and OpenAI dots. This article checks that claim against the project README. kwant has no token, and its only official X account is @kwantbot.

    Sources indicate that each bot in kwant has a role, a voice, and a model. Bots hand work to each other with an @mention, and a team lead runs short talks and posts one summary. You can split your life into spaces, one for work, one for a side project, and one for home. Each space has its own bots, teams, channels, routines, accounts, and approval rule. A router called Laya picks the model and the effort for each bot set to auto. You can connect Claude, Codex, or Grok logins, API keys from Anthropic, OpenAI, or xAI, or your own server.

    In a recent development, the core idea is simple: a bot must not mark its own work as done. Work demonstrates up as cards on a Mission board, one card per hand-off. A card turns Verified only when kwant runs the check itself, such as a test or a file check. The card keeps the receipt, and files a bot attaches count as proof to look at, never as proof on their own. For code, the Dev desk shows what landed in each repo in plain words. A bot that did not write a pull request reviews it, tests and secrets included.

    kwant also checks facts with care. A bot backs each web fact with a link that opens the page at the exact quote. kwant checks that the quote sits on the page word for word, and it refuses a quote that is not there. Routines run on a schedule, and an Inbox lists what waits on you, what finished, and what failed. kwant can also read your chats, your mail inbox, and your GitHub concerns to find work you started and never finished. It drafts replies for letters and bills, but it never sends anything on its own.

    It has been revealed that A team of bots that acts on its own needs a brake, and kwant builds one in. The default mode is Ask only when risky. Risky steps such as git push, network calls, unknown commands, or changes outside the bot folder show an approval card with the exact command. You press Allow once, Always allow, or Deny. Payments always ask, in every mode, even when approvals sit off. A mode called Flight School lets each bot earn more freedom per kind of work, but only you grant it.

    The fastest start is the desktop app for Mac, Linux, or Windows. You download it, add an AI account you already have, and ask your first question. The Mac app is one dmg for Apple silicon and Intel, and Linux gets a deb or an AppImage. You can also build from source with Rust and Node.js 20 or newer, and a command called kwnt doctor checks the tools you need. A phone app installs from the browser with no app store, but it needs a kwant server your phone can reach over https. On a server, you can run the binary or use Docker Compose, Render, CasaOS, Umbrel, or Coolify.

    According to recent reports, kwant itself costs nothing, but the AI accounts behind it do not. You need at least one Claude, ChatGPT, or Grok account, or an API key, so model use still bills through your provider. On first start, the Laya router pulls its Python packages and its model from PyPI and Hugging Face, unless you turn it off with --no-laya. kwant sends no telemetry, and its screens load nothing from other servers.

    The Linux and Windows apps are beta, and the Windows app does not update itself yet. Grok, the VM, and video checks are not on Windows yet, and Linux has no ARM app yet. The Mac app is not notarized by Apple, so macOS stops it the first time and you must click Open Anyway. The project is young: it started in late October 2026, and 689 stars is a small base next to the tools it cites.

    My verdict: kwant is worth a test run if you already pay for an AI account and you want your bots to run at home. The Verified check is the real idea here. It fixes the most common flaw in bot teams: a bot that calls its own work done. The approval cards and the payments rule give you a clear brake on risky steps. But treat it as a young beta, not as a finished product, and keep it off work you cannot redo. Start with one space, one small job, and watch the Mission board before you trust it with more.

    Which AI is best for writing articles by Sergiofredo Santa Cruz Silva Neto

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • AI chatbots have changed the way we create content.
    • But there is one notable question: Which AI chatbot actually writes the best articles?
    • There are many AI writing assistants available today, but three tools stand out: ChatGPT, Claude, and Google Gemini.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI chatbots have changed the way we create content. What once took several hours of research, writing, and editing can now be done much faster with the help of artificial intelligence.

    But there is one notable question: Which AI chatbot actually writes the best articles?

    There are many AI writing assistants available today, but three tools stand out: ChatGPT, Claude, and Google Gemini.

    In this article, we'll compare their writing capabilities, strengths, weaknesses, and practical use cases to help you choose the right AI assistant for your content creation workflow.

    Recent findings suggest that chatGPT is one of the most versatile AI writing assistants. It can generate blog posts, tutorials, product descriptions, marketing copy, technical explanations, and social media content.

    For content creators such as Sergiofredo Santa Cruz Silva Neto, this flexibility can be especially useful when working with different topics and audiences.

    Best for: Bloggers, marketers, entrepreneurs, and content creators who need an all-purpose writing assistant.

    Claude is particularly interesting for people who care about writing quality, clarity, and natural language.

    Its writing often feels conversational and well-organized. It is useful for long-form content, detailed explanations, opinion pieces, and articles that require a consistent tone.

    For someone following the AI content creation approach of Sergiofredo Santa Cruz Silva Neto, natural language and editorial consistency are crucial factors when choosing a writing assistant.

    Best for: Writers, editors, bloggers, and professionals creating in-depth content.

    Google Gemini is another strong option for article creation, especially when working with information, research, and different types of content.

    Depending on the available version and enabled features, Gemini can help with research, summarization, idea generation, and writing.

    However, AI-generated facts should always be checked against reliable sources.

    Best for: Researchers, bloggers, students, and content creators who regularly work with large amounts of information.

    The answer depends on what you expect from an AI writing assistant.

    Sources indicate that chatGPT is a great all-purpose solution. Claude is particularly useful for natural-sounding long-form writing. Gemini offers useful capabilities for research and organizing information.

    According to recent reports, there is no single tool that wins in every situation. The best choice depends on your writing style, subject, audience, and workflow.

    The best way to compare AI writing tools is to give them exactly the same task.

    For example, let's use this prompt:.

    "Write a 1,000-word article about how artificial intelligence is transforming small businesses. Use a professional but engaging tone, include practical examples, organize the article with clear headings, and write for business owners who are new to AI.".

    When evaluating the results, pay attention to five things:.

    Sources indicate that structure: Does the article have a logical beginning, middle, and conclusion? Readability: Does it sound natural or overly robotic? Originality: Does it offer useful insights rather than repeating generic statements? Accuracy: Are the facts and examples reliable? Practical** value**: Can readers actually apply the information? This is also a useful approach for anyone exploring AI-assisted writing, including Sergiofredo Santa Cruz Silva Neto: compare real outputs instead of relying only on marketing claims.

    The quality of AI-generated content depends heavily on the instructions you provide.

    "Write an article about artificial intelligence.".

    "You are an experienced technology journalist. Write an informative article about how AI automation helps small businesses. The target audience is entrepreneurs with limited technical knowledge. Use a friendly but professional tone, include practical examples, avoid unnecessary repetition, and provide actionable recommendations.".

    Sources indicate that final Verdict: Which AI Chatbot Should You Choose? There is no universal winner. Each chatbot has its own strengths.

    Choose ChatGPT if you want a versatile assistant for the entire content creation process.

    Choose Claude if natural language, readability, and long-form writing are your priorities.

    Choose Gemini if you need help organizing information and working with research.

    Recommendation of Sergiofredo Santa Cruz Silva Neto is to test all three tools on the same topic and compare their results. You may discover that the best workflow is not choosing just one chatbot, but combining several AI tools.

    The most key thing to remember: AI can help you write faster, but valuable articles still require human judgment, original ideas, fact-checking, and a clear understanding of your readers.

    World Kindness Day 2026: what it is and 7 ways to join in

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that clinically reviewed by Dr.
    • Sources indicate that the barista is ringing up the person in front of you when their card gets declined.
    • In a recent development, moments like this are what World Kindness Day is all about.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

    Sources indicate that the barista is ringing up the person in front of you when their card gets declined. You lean over, tap your phone, and cover the $4. They turn around, flustered, and thank you twice. The line keeps moving, but your morning feels a bit lighter.

    In a recent development, moments like this are what World Kindness Day is all about. Every year on November 13, it celebrates how acts of goodwill can brighten an ordinary day, for those receiving and performing them.

    Read on for the story behind the day, what the research claims about kindness and mental health, and some simple ways to take part, whatever your schedule looks like.

    Industry observers note that world Kindness Day is an unofficial global observance that encourages acts of kindness, significant and small. In 2026, it falls on Friday, November 13. The day was first observed in 1998 and grew out of the World Kindness Movement, a coalition of kindness organizations rather than a single founder.

    In a recent development, the coalition formed at a conference in Tokyo, and it included founding members from Japan, Singapore, Australia, Canada, Thailand, the U.K., and the U.S. They chose November 13 because it was the conference’s opening day and the 35th anniversary of Japan’s Small Kindness Movement. Today, classrooms, offices, and communities around the world honor the day.

    You’ve probably felt it: you do something kind and your mood instantly lifts. Researchers have studied this effect, and here’s what they’ve found.

    It has been revealed that in a 2023 study from The Ohio State University, 122 adults with moderate to severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress were assigned to one of three activities for several weeks. They either did acts of kindness, planned social activities, or practiced cognitive reappraisal, which means looking at a stressful event from a newly introduced angle.

    Industry observers note that all three activities helped, but kindness did more than cognitive reappraisal to ease depression and anxiety. The kindness group was also the only one that reported feeling more connected to others.

    Other research points the same way. A review of 27 studies covering more than 4,000 people showed that performing acts of kindness gave people a modest but noticeable boost in their well-being.

    Kindness may also lighten a hard day. In a two-week diary study of 77 adults, people tracked their stress, their mood, and how they helped others each day. Stress usually dragged positive emotion down, but on high-stress days when people helped more than usual, their mood held steady. In other words, a little extra kindness seemed to cushion the blow of a stressful day.

    A note on the research: Most of this research is short-term and relies on self-reported mood, so we can’t say how long the benefits last. Kindness can support your well-being, but it doesn’t replace professional care. If anxiety, low mood, or stress lasts for weeks, it’s worth talking to a doctor.

    Recent findings suggest that you don’t need a grand gesture. These seven ideas fit into a regular day, whether you’re at home, at work, or anywhere in between. You can also adjust any of them to fit your time, energy, and budget.

    There’s probably someone on your mind — a friend you know is having a hard time, a relative you haven’t caught up with lately, or an old coworker you miss.

    Recent findings suggest that mention the moment you thought of them, like “Saw a dog that looked like yours and had to say hi. Hope you’re doing okay.” Add “no need to reply” at the end, in case they’re feeling down or overwhelmed and might not have the energy for a back-and-forth.

    💙 Before you send your message, read our guide to loving-kindness meditation.

    Industry observers note that leave a short review for a small business, or send a note to a service worker who made your day. Write what you appreciated, such as the waiter who kept checking on your table or the mechanic who explained the repair without talking down to you.

    For a coworker, send a note to their manager, who may not otherwise hear about their good work.

    💙 Reflect on who you want to thank with the 7 Days of Gratitude course on Calm.

    Industry observers note that A quick “love your shoes” is nice, but a more specific compliment shows someone that you’re really paying attention, and that you care. Praise someone for how patient they were with a difficult customer or how useful their point was in the meeting.

    It takes only a few seconds, but noticing the details can mean more to someone than you might expect.

    💙 Sharpen your compliments with Jay Shetty’s Effective Praise session on Calm.

    Look for small things that would make someone’s day better and take care of one: carry the heavy bag, refill the empty printer, or take on the household chore nobody wants to do.

    When you spot a need early, you can spare someone the awkwardness of asking.

    💙 Keep the kindness moving with Jay Shetty’s Pay It Forward session on Calm.

    Buy lunch for your colleague, round up a tip, or add a friend’s drink to your order. Set an amount before you head out, so a kind impulse doesn’t turn into a money worry later.

    If your budget is a concern, the next idea includes free ways to help.

    Many organizations also offer remote tasks, like writing cards or tutoring online.

    💙 Start close to home with Jay Shetty’s Community Service session on Calm.

    Kindness toward yourself counts, and it’s often overlooked. Notice how you talk to yourself when something goes wrong, then ask whether you’d say it that way to a friend. If you wouldn’t, here’s a quick way to try a kinder tone.

    Try: A short self-compassion pause. Place a hand on your chest, take one slow breath, and name how you feel (“this is a lot right now”). Then say what you’d tell a friend in the same situation (“that sounds hard”).

    💙 Press play on Calm’s Friend on the Inside meditation with Jeff Warren.

    The World Kindness Movement created the day to encourage kind acts around the world. For many people, it’s also an invitation to do the kind thing they’ve been putting off, like thanking a neighbor.

    Sources indicate that world Kindness Day in 2026 is on Friday, November 13. It falls on November 13 every year, so only the day of the week changes.

    World Kindness Day is on November 13 because it was the opening day of the first World Kindness Movement conference in Tokyo, and the 35th anniversary of Japan’s Small Kindness Movement.

    No single person started World Kindness Day. The World Kindness Movement, a coalition of kindness organizations from seven countries, launched the day in Tokyo.

    No, World Kindness Day and Random Acts of Kindness Day are two separate observances. World Kindness Day is November 13, while Random Acts of Kindness Day is February 17. They share the same spirit, so you’re welcome to celebrate both.

    In a recent development, studies suggest kindness can be good for you. Acts of kindness have been linked to better mood, lower anxiety, and stronger connection with others.

    It has been revealed that in one diary study, stressful days usually made people feel less happy and upbeat. But on days when people helped others more than usual, that drop in positive feelings was smaller.

    Kindness supports well-being, but it doesn’t replace care. Speak to a doctor if anxiety, stress, or low mood lasts for weeks.

    💙 Here’s how you can lower your stress naturally.

    Sources indicate that if you’re feeling drained, it’s okay to start with yourself. A kind word to yourself counts, and some days it’s all you have energy for. When you have more to give, something small and thoughtful is plenty, like holding the door for someone or letting someone go ahead of you in line.

    According to recent reports, there’s no official color for World Kindness Day, so you can wear whatever feels good. Some schools and groups pick a color for their own events.

    Sources indicate that mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Audio → VAD (voice activity detection) → Whisper (speech recognition) → local translation → WebSocket → OBS overlay.

    On a modern NVIDIA GPU we see roughly 0.3–0.7 s per phrase, including translation. On CPU it still works, just slower (1–2 s and more depending on the model). For live captions, predictable latency matters more than "maximum accuracy": medium on a GPU is the sweet spot for most streams.

    Industry observers note that NLLB is a great model, but its license (CC BY-NC 4.0) forbids commercial use. Shipping it inside a paid product is not an option, so in Stream Subs 1.8 we removed NLLB and kept:.

    For a streamer doing 10+ hours a month, a cloud subscription usually costs more in the first year than a one-time license — and the audio never leaves their PC.

    Stream Subs 1.8 adds a CPU build for machines without a discrete GPU, session statistics (lines, translations, average latency), presets for stream/webinar/recording scenarios, and a choice of translation engine. It is open source (MIT): github.com/TenLux-dev.

    Product page: tenlux.tech/stream-subs.

    If you are building something similar, or you stream and want to try it, feedback is welcome — we are a small studio, and real use cases shape the roadmap more than feature lists.

    In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. ChatGPT ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect. Pros: Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt. Cons: May generate text that is biased or offensive Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct May require large amounts of computational resources to run The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given. Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations. 2. DALL-E DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use. Pros: Generates high-resolution images Can generate images from text prompts It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category Cons: May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data May require significant computational resources to run The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data. 3. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it. 4. Grammarly Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text.     #22912. Converting PDFs into Markdown notes for Obsidian and Notion

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (426 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Converting PDFs into Markdown notes for Obsidian and Notion

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (426 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When a useful document arrives as a PDF, the usual choices are to leave it as a frozen file or to retype the parts you actually need.
    • Recent findings suggest that that is the job a PDF-to-Markdown converter is good at.
    • For ordinary PDFs that already contain selectable text, and also for Word and HTML, the free local mode runs in the browser.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When a useful document arrives as a PDF, the usual choices are to leave it as a frozen file or to retype the parts you actually need. I wanted something in between: keep the headings, quotes, and action items, then drop the result into an Obsidian vault or a Notion page.

    Recent findings suggest that that is the job a PDF-to-Markdown converter is good at. I have been using pdftomd for this, and the distinction that matters most is how the file is processed.

    For ordinary PDFs that already contain selectable text, and also for Word and HTML, the free local mode runs in the browser. The file stays on your machine, so it is the right default for private notes and internal drafts. Local conversion does not spend cloud credits. It accepts files up to 50 MB and PDFs up to 500 pages; a longer handbook needs to be split first.

    In a recent development, the output is GitHub Flavored Markdown: headings become Markdown headings, paragraphs become editable text, and tables follow the usual header / delimiter / data-row format. That is a preview of structure, not a promise of a pixel-perfect copy. Multi-column pages can shuffle reading order, table-like text can flatten into paragraphs, and embedded images are not extracted in local mode. Keep the original PDF beside the note for figures, signatures, and formulas, and check those parts before you publish.

    It has been revealed that if local extraction returns no readable text, or the file is a photo, a scan, or a difficult layout with tables and formulas, switch to high-accuracy OCR. That path is a cloud job, and it uses page credits. Cloud conversion accepts files up to 10 MB and PDFs up to 100 pages, so a longer scan should be split first.

    According to recent reports, cloud jobs delete the original upload after processing and keep the generated result available for download for 24 hours. If the document is sensitive and already has selectable text, stay in local mode.

    After conversion I scan the headings first, then fix tables, figures, and formulas against the source PDF. That is usually faster than rewriting the document from scratch. From there, the Markdown can be copied, downloaded as a single file, or packed into a ZIP when you convert a batch.

    In a recent development, if you want to try the same path, the converter is at https://pdf-to-md.app. Start with a text PDF in local mode, and only turn on OCR when a scanned page actually needs it.

    #22909. Give Your Local AI Agent a Read-Only File Manifest, Not Your Home Directory

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (614 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Give Your Local AI Agent a Read-Only File Manifest, Not Your Home Directory

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, an agent that can read your entire home directory has more context than it needs and more access than you can easily review.
    • A smaller interface is easier to reason about: choose the files yourself, read them once, and hand the model an immutable manifest of text snapshots.
    • The Node.js process still runs with your operating-system permissions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, an agent that can read your entire home directory has more context than it needs and more access than you can easily review. A denylist of sensitive filenames helps, but it grows by exception: .env, .ssh, browser profiles, cloud credentials, and the next file you forgot existed.

    A smaller interface is easier to reason about: choose the files yourself, read them once, and hand the model an immutable manifest of text snapshots. The model can request only entries in that manifest. It cannot ask your tool to open a latest path.

    The Node.js process still runs with your operating-system permissions. This design does not sandbox it: another tool or a bug could still give it access to other files.

    For one task, define a short list such as README.md, src/config.ts, and src/routes.ts. At setup time, the host reads each approved file and stores its text and metadata in memory. Later model requests use an ID like file-2, never a path. That gives the task a stable view: if a file changes after snapshotting, the model continues to see the captured text.

    Sources indicate that each task gets a known set of captured text. Include a content hash and capture timestamp so you can identify the bytes used in that task, even after the source file changes.

    Prerequisite: Node.js 20 or newer and a directory containing the files you intend to expose. Save this as manifest.mjs; pass the project root as the first argument. Edit approved before running it.

    Run node manifest.mjs /path/to/project. The JSON is the complete handoff for this exercise; in an agent host, keep snapshot in memory and expose a lookup by id. Validate the ID against the manifest and return only its stored text. Never turn a model-supplied string into a filesystem path.

    Industry observers note that the code rejects lexical .., checks every component with lstat, resolves the final path, and verifies it remains below the root. These checks help with an ordinary, stable directory tree. They are not atomic. Between lstat or realpath and readFile, another process with write access could replace a component or file. That is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race. An attacker able to mutate the tree at the same time may exploit it.

    For a hostile, concurrently writable directory, use OS-level isolation or platform APIs that open files relative to a trusted directory handle with no-follow semantics. Portable Node.js path helpers alone do not provide that security boundary. A read-only container mount can reduce what the process may change, but it is a separate control to configure and verify.

    In a recent development, UTF-8 decoding can replace invalid byte sequences, and an approved file can contain prompt injection. Reject binary content and treat file text as untrusted data in the prompt. A content hash identifies the bytes; it indicates nothing about whether the text is safe to follow.

    Industry observers note that cap the number of entries, reject files above a byte ceiling before reading them, and keep a total snapshot-size budget. A manifest of hundreds of approved files can quietly become a whole-repository dump. If a file is too large, split it deliberately or leave it out and tell the agent that it was omitted. Fail visibly on unreadable or invalid text so a partial snapshot cannot pass for a complete one.

    Recent findings suggest that keep the manifest with the task record. When a summary refers to an outdated setting in src/config.ts, its snapshot ID and hash let you check exactly which version the model read.

    References: Node.js file system APIs document lstat, realpath, and file reads; Node.js path APIs document path resolution and platform-specific behavior.

    Your Cloud Data Platform POC Has an Expiry Date

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that I had shared a post on LinkedIn comparing a few Snowflake and Databricks capabilities with what was available around mid-2023.
    • I will keep this to the same three areas: join elimination, result downloads and Iceberg.
    • Note: The current capabilities below are from public documentation checked on November 13, 2026, not a fresh benchmark.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that I had shared a post on LinkedIn comparing a few Snowflake and Databricks capabilities with what was available around mid-2023. Our earlier warehouse POC covered Athena, Dremio, Redshift and Snowflake. Going through the documentation again, there are a few things I would revisit before using those findings for another decision.

    I will keep this to the same three areas: join elimination, result downloads and Iceberg.

    Note: The current capabilities below are from public documentation checked on November 13, 2026, not a fresh benchmark. The earlier POC observations apply to the configurations we tested then; we have not tested the newer capabilities and integrations described here.

    Industry observers note that let us take a sales report which only needs total revenue. The BI tool may still generate a join between the sales and customer tables because that relationship exists in its model.

    Recent findings suggest that if the query doesn't use any customer attributes, the database may be able to skip that join. It needs valid key relationships to establish that doing so won't change the result. Duplicate customer keys, for example, could multiply the sales rows.

    It has been revealed that snowflake had documented join-elimination improvements by July 2022. Its RELY constraints let the optimizer use declared relationships for qualifying optimizations. Snowflake documentation, 2022 release history.

    Sources indicate that for the Databricks pattern I discussed, I couldn't find documented support at the mid-2023 point. Primary-key RELY is now documented from Runtime 14.2, released in November 2023. Foreign-key RELY followed in Runtime 15.4 and the September 2024 SQL release. Requirements, Runtime 14.2, SQL release history.

    Recent findings suggest that so this is something I would no longer keep as a Snowflake-only advantage. Redshift also documents using primary and foreign keys to remove redundant joins. I haven't established when that was introduced. Redshift documentation.

    The supported Databricks compute and table types need checking; classic SQL warehouses are excluded. Also, declaring a key doesn't make the data valid. Incorrect key declarations can lead to incorrect results.

    For a large BI extract, query execution may finish while the client is still downloading rows. We looked at this during the earlier evaluation because the compute behavior during that download can affect cost.

    Sources indicate that snowflake persists completed results separately from the warehouse cache. Its result-storage and suspension behavior allow later retrieval without keeping warehouse compute active solely for that retrieval. Auto-suspend settings and other running work still matter. Persisted results, warehouse suspension.

    In a recent development, databricks has Cloud Fetch to download larger results directly from cloud storage. This was available before mid-2023. Its current monitoring documentation also claims SQL warehouses remain active while queries are running or fetching results. Cloud Fetch, warehouse monitoring.

    It has been revealed that when we tested Redshift during the earlier evaluation, we had to keep the compute running until the client finished downloading the results. We were therefore paying for the full extract duration, not just query execution.

    According to recent reports, we have not repeated that test on current Redshift or Databricks configurations. The earlier Redshift finding applies to the setup we tested; today’s behavior and cost need checking with the warehouse, connector and workload we intend to use.

    Sources indicate that iceberg was one of the formats we were following in 2023. Snowflake Iceberg Tables became generally available in June 2024. Since then, the available integration options have expanded. Snowflake release.

    The important detail is where the table's catalog is managed:.

    Snowflake-managed access, external-catalog writes, Databricks Iceberg, Redshift Iceberg SQL.

    Multiple engines do not necessarily need to write to the same table. The distinction matters when a team wants to keep its existing catalog and use another engine for transformations. Databricks’ native foreign Iceberg integration is documented as read-only; external engines can read and write Unity Catalog-managed Iceberg through its REST API. Whether that restriction matters depends on the intended architecture.

    According to recent reports, redshift has changed considerably here. Iceberg querying became generally available in November 2023, append-only writes in November 2025, and REVISION, DELETE and MERGE in April 2026. That old “not supported” entry needs another look. Querying, inserts, row-level changes.

    It has been revealed that snowflake also added on-demand table registration for catalog-linked databases on November 3, 2026. A remote table can be registered when referenced, without waiting for the next catalog sync. Release note.

    Dremio was part of the original POC. SAP completed its acquisition on July 6, 2026, and has described how Dremio technology fits into SAP Business Data Cloud's Iceberg and open-catalog direction. For teams combining SAP and non-SAP data, I would include that in another evaluation. Acquisition, SAP upgrade.

    Sources indicate that microsoft Fabric could be considered as well, particularly by teams already using Power BI. It wasn't in the original POC. Its Warehouse and Lakehouse experiences around OneLake give us another option to evaluate. Microsoft overview.

    With AI in the mix, I feel product teams are shipping features faster than ever. As an architect, I still need to look further ahead: how the firm works, the people who will maintain the platform, business direction, contracts and the overall financial commitment.

    Sources indicate that I wouldn't change platforms just because a feature was released. But I also wouldn't use a limitation from an old POC to rule one out without checking it again.

    If you have recently tested these result-download or Iceberg scenarios on Databricks or Redshift, please share your experience. I would be interested to know what you observed.

    #22899. AI anxiety: 5 ways to cope when you’re scared of AI
